content:
Christian apologists sometimes cite Quran 43:61 as a hidden confession. The verse says of Jesus (peace be upon him) that he is "knowledge of the Hour", they argue, and knowledge of the Hour belongs to God alone, so the Quran gives Jesus a divine attribute.[1]

The verse is real and its wording is disputed. The classical commentators debated its pronoun and its reading for centuries, and their debate is on record.

This article aims to provide context to the claim, insha'Allah, in five points drawn from the verse's context, its readings and its commentators. The Quran's own description of Jesus, four verses earlier, frames them: "He was no more than a servant: We granted Our favour to him, and We made him an example to the Children of Israel" (43:59).[2]

Quran 43:57 to 65 is one passage about Jesus. It opens with the Quraysh mocking when "(Jesus) the son of Mary is held up as an example" (43:57), and it calls him "no more than a servant" (43:59).[2]

After verse 61 Jesus speaks for himself: "therefore fear Allah and obey me. For Allah, He is my Lord and your Lord: so worship ye Him: this is a Straight Way" (43:63 to 64).[2] A verse placed between "no more than a servant" and "my Lord and your Lord" would be a strange place for the Quran to declare him God.

The verse begins wa-innahu la-ʿilmun li-l-sāʿah, "and indeed he (or it) is knowledge of the Hour". Al-Ṭabarī says the commentators "differed over the pronoun" in innahu.[3]

Most of the authorities he cites read it as Jesus: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd all explain it as his coming down "before the Day of Resurrection". Others, al-Ḥasan among them, read it as the Quran, which gives knowledge of the Hour and its terrors.[3]

On either reading the verse speaks of knowing that the Hour is coming. On neither does it make Jesus the One who knows its time, which the Quran reserves to God: "with Him is the Knowledge of the Hour (of Judgment)" (43:85).[2]

The reciters of every region read la-ʿilmun, "knowledge", and al-Ṭabarī judges it the correct reading "because the authorities among the reciters agree on it". He also records that Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read la-ʿalamun, "a sign" or "a marker", and that the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read "a reminder (dhikr) of the Hour".[3]

The reading "sign" explains the English translations. A. Yusuf Ali renders the verse: "And (Jesus) shall be a Sign (for the coming of) the Hour (of Judgment): therefore have no doubt about the (Hour), but follow ye Me".[2] His brackets show the reading he follows, and the word he chooses is the one al-Ṭabarī's authorities used.

Gabriel Said Reynolds, a Christian scholar of the Quran, has studied the verse and its readings in his article on whether the Muslim Jesus is dead or alive.[4] The debate he traces concerns the end of Jesus' life and his return, and divinity has no place in it.

Ibn Kathīr writes that "the correct view concerning this phrase is that it refers to his descent before the Day of Resurrection", and joins it to 4:159: "there is none of the People of the Book but must believe in him before his death".[5]

He reports the same reading from Abu Hurayra and Ibn ʿAbbās. The hadith behind it is in al-Bukhari: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) saying that the son of Mary will descend as a just ruler, break the cross and kill the swine, and Abu Hurayra then recites 4:159.[6]

A sign of the Hour is a creature God sends before it. The Quran calls many created things signs (āyāt), the night and the day among them, and none of them is God for being a sign. We set out what Muslims believe about the last days in 5 things Muslims believe about the end of time.

Islam honours Jesus above most of creation. He is the Messiah, born without a father, a worker of miracles by God's leave, and a sign of the Hour. The same Quran that grants all of this denies him divinity in plain words.

"They do blaspheme who say: 'Allah is Christ the son of Mary.' But said Christ: 'O Children of Israel! worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord'" (5:72). He and his mother "had both to eat their (daily) food" (5:75).[2]

God brings the Hour and alone knows its time. Jesus' return, on the reading of most commentators, is one of its signs. A sign points to its Lord, and Jesus' own words in this surah point the same way.

The bottom line

Quran 43:61 is a disputed verse, and the dispute is about its pronoun and its reading. The commentators read it as Jesus' descent before the Resurrection or as the Quran's teaching about the Hour, and read ʿilm, "knowledge", or ʿalam, "sign". None of them read it as making Jesus God, and the passage around it calls him a servant who says "my Lord and your Lord".

The argument from 43:61 asks a sign to be the Lord it points to. The Quran's answer, in the same surah, is the one Jesus gives: "Allah, He is my Lord and your Lord: so worship ye Him" (43:64).[2] We set out the wider case in 5 reasons why Muslims believe that Jesus is not God. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. The argument draws on the Quran's statement that knowledge of the Hour is with God (43:85; 31:34). The Bismikaa archive answered it in Membongkar Kebobrokan Penafsiran Surah Az-Zukhruf, Ayat 61.
  2. Quran 43:57 to 65; 43:85; 5:72 to 75, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, on Quran 43:61, Arabic text read on quran.com; the English is our translation.
  4. Gabriel Said Reynolds, "The Muslim Jesus: Dead or Alive?", Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 72, no. 2 (2009), pp. 237–258, doi:10.1017/S0041977X09000500.
  5. Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, on Quran 43:61, abridged English translation on quran.com; Quran 4:159, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 3448, from Abu Hurayra (numbering of sunnah.com).
